prompt: Before we onboard another outside service, I want the roles we already give outsiders tightened. The trust and permission policies are under infra/roles/: monitoring, backup, partner CI, and our own cross-account deploy role. The onboarding records in docs/integrations/ (one page per party) and config/accounts.json are the source of truth for who may assume each role and under what conditions; do not change them. Make each trust policy accept exactly who its page says, under the conditions its page gives, and nothing else. The monitoring vendor only reads metrics and logs for a dashboard, so cut its permission policy down to that. Leave the other permission policies alone. Keep every file valid IAM policy JSON, keep npm test, npm run lint and scripts/check-iam.js working, and add no dependencies.

items.text: Explains that the external id protects against a vendor being tricked into using our role for another customer, so it is required for third parties and not needed for our own deploy account.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, Access to AWS accounts owned by third parties, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_common-scenarios_third-party.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Spots that the monitoring policy allowed everything except the listed read actions (a NotAction allow) and says why that inverted the intent.
Explains that the organization condition keeps the deploy role usable only from inside our organization even if an account id is reused or misconfigured.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, The confused deputy problem, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Suggests a reusable pattern or check for the new vendor (named principal, external id, read-only scope, review date) so the next onboarding does not repeat these gaps.

verdicts.note: The prompt names deliverables (tighten role policies, update trust documents) but does not prescribe a methodology like TDD, threat modeling, or a checklist.

All hidden tests rely only on values explicitly stated in the docs (account IDs, role names, external IDs, organization ID) or behaviors the prompt directly specifies (allow AssumeRole and TagSession, deny SetSourceIdentity, read-only CloudWatch/Logs).
The fixture contains no hints about defects; the docs are authoritative integration records, and the existing tests check unrelated utility functions.
Reviewer passed it, but the draft prompt listed every fix. The lead rewrote it to point at the onboarding pages as the source of truth; 17 of 90 hidden tests pass on the fixture.
Every hidden test checks a behavior the prompt explicitly requires or follows directly from documented values; a careful engineer who reads the docs and follows AWS IAM patterns can pass all tests.

rubric.criterion: The final message explains the design of each trust condition so the next onboarding can copy it. Fail: lists the changes with no reason, or gives a wrong reason (for example says the external id protects our own deploy role). Partial: explains one of: why the vendor roles need an external id (confused deputy), why the organisation condition is there, why a role ARN rather than an account root is trusted; quoted. Pass: explains all three correctly, scopes log reads to named log groups or says why not, and gives a check or template the next vendor goes through. (code cannot check this because the hidden tests check which principals are accepted, not whether the reasons are right or reusable)
